nodes.statement: The $i$-th round of sum-check consists of: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Input:} A statement containing target value and prior challenges, along with an oracle for the multivariate polynomial \item \textbf{Prover's message:} A univariate polynomial $p_i \in R[X]_{\leq d}$ \item \textbf{Verifier's challenge:} A random element $r_i \gets R$ \item \textbf{Output:} An updated statement with new target $p_i(r_i)$ and extended challenges \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: One sum-check round: prover sends p_i, verifier sends r_i, output new target p_i(r_i) with extended challenges.
nodes.label: def:sumcheck_single_round

nodes.name: Single Round Completeness
nodes.statement: Each individual round of the sum-check protocol is perfectly complete.
conclusions: Each individual round of the sum-check protocol is perfectly complete.
nodes.label: thm:sumcheck_single_round_completeness

nodes.name: Single Round Soundness
nodes.statement: Each individual round of the sum-check protocol is sound with error probability at most $d / |R|$, where $d$ is the degree bound and $|R|$ is the size of the field.
conclusions: Each individual round of the sum-check protocol is sound with error probability at most $d / |R|$
nodes.label: thm:sumcheck_single_round_soundness

nodes.name: Round-by-Round Knowledge Soundness
nodes.statement: The sum-check protocol satisfies round-by-round knowledge soundness. Each individual round can be analyzed independently, and the soundness error in each round is bounded by $d / |R|$.
conclusions: The sum-check protocol satisfies round-by-round knowledge soundness.
the soundness error in each round is bounded by $d / |R|$
nodes.label: thm:sumcheck_rbr_knowledge_soundness

nodes.name: Virtual sum-check round protocol
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item In this protocol, the context is a pair $(p, d)$, where $p$ is now a \emph{univariate} polynomial of bounded degree. The predicate / relation is that $p(0) + p(1) = d$. \item The prover first sends a univariate polynomial $s$ of the same bounded degree as $p$. In the honest case, it would just send $p$ itself. \item The verifier samples and sends a random challenge $r \gets R$. \item The verifier checks that $s(0) + s(1) = d$. The predicate on the resulting output context is that $p(r) = s(r)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Univariate sum-check round: prover sends s, verifier sends r and checks s(0)+s(1)=d; output predicate p(r)=s(r).
nodes.label: def:virtual_sumcheck_round_protocol

nodes.name: Emulating a sum-check round by the virtual protocol
nodes.statement: The reason why this simpler protocol is related to a sum-check round is that we can \emph{emulate} the simpler protocol using variables in the context at the time: \begin{itemize} \item The univariate polynomial $p$ is instantiated as $\sum_{x \in (\text{Image}(\mathcal{D}))^{n - i - 1}} P(r_0, \ldots, r_{i - 1}, X, x)$. \item The scalar $d$ is instantiated as $T$ if $i = 0$, and as $s_{i - 1}(r_{i - 1})$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Each sum-check round instantiates the virtual protocol with p the partial sum and d the previous target.

nodes.name: Virtual sum-check round is perfectly complete
nodes.statement: It is "clear" that the simpler protocol is perfectly complete.

nodes.name: Proof of virtual round soundness (Schwartz-Zippel)
nodes.statement: It is sound (and since there is no witness, also knowledge sound) since by the Schwartz-Zippel Lemma, the probability that $p \ne s$ and yet $p(r) = s(r)$ for a random challenge $r$ is at most the degree of $p$ over the size of the field.
nodes.statement_short: Schwartz-Zippel: distinct p, s agree at a random r with probability at most deg(p)/|F|.

nodes.name: Virtual sum-check round protocol is sound
nodes.statement: The virtual sum-check round protocol is sound.
conclusions: The virtual sum-check round protocol is sound.
nodes.label: thm:virtual_sumcheck_round_protocol_sound

nodes.name: Proof of virtual round knowledge soundness
nodes.statement: Note that there is no witness, so knowledge soundness follows trivially from soundness.
nodes.statement_short: No witness, so knowledge soundness reduces to soundness.

nodes.name: Virtual sum-check round protocol is knowledge sound
nodes.statement: The virtual sum-check round protocol is knowledge sound.
conclusions: The virtual sum-check round protocol is knowledge sound.
nodes.label: thm:virtual_sumcheck_round_protocol_knowledge_sound

nodes.name: State Function
nodes.statement: The state function for the virtual sum-check round protocol is given by: \begin{enumerate} \item The initial state function is the same as the predicate on the initial context, namely that $p(0) + p(1) = d$. \item The state function after the prover sends $s$ is the predicate that $p(0) + p(1) = d$ and $s(0) + s(1) = d$. Essentially, we add in the verifier's check. \item The state function for the output context (after the verifier sends $r$) is the predicate that $s(0) + s(1) = d$ and $p(r) = s(r)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.definiendum: state function for the virtual sum-check round protocol
nodes.statement_short: State function: initial predicate, then add the verifier's check, then s(0)+s(1)=d and p(r)=s(r).
nodes.label: def:virtual_sumcheck_round_protocol_state_function

nodes.name: Proof of virtual round RBR soundness
nodes.statement: Seen in this light, it should be clear that the simpler protocol satisfies round-by-round soundness.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the state function just defined.

nodes.name: Virtual sum-check round protocol is round-by-round sound
nodes.statement: The virtual sum-check round protocol is round-by-round sound.
conclusions: The virtual sum-check round protocol is round-by-round sound.
nodes.label: thm:virtual_sumcheck_round_protocol_rbr_sound

nodes.name: Ring switching
nodes.statement: \emph{Ring switching} is a reduction that turns a multilinear evaluation claim over a \emph{small} coefficient ring $B$ into an evaluation claim over a \emph{large} extension $L$, paying only an additive $O(1/\lvert L\rvert)$ soundness cost and \emph{without re-committing} over $L$.

nodes.name: Ring-switching profile
nodes.statement: Fix commutative rings $B$ (small) and $L$ (large) with $L$ a $B$-algebra, and $\kappa \in \mathbb{N}$. A \emph{ring-switching profile} consists of: \begin{itemize} \item a rank-$2^\kappa$ $B$-basis $\beta = (\beta_u)_{u \in \{0,1\}^\kappa}$ of $L$; \item a commutative \emph{pack/trace carrier} $A$ that is an $L$-algebra (the type sent on the wire); \item two ring homomorphisms $\varphi_0, \varphi_1 : L \to A$ for evaluation-point data and polynomial coefficients, respectively; \item coordinate maps $\mathrm{decomposeColumns}, \mathrm{decomposeRows} : A \to (\{0,1\}^\kappa \to L)$; \item subject to the two \emph{reconstruction laws} \begin{equation} z = \sum_{u} \varphi_0(\beta_u)\cdot \varphi_1(\mathrm{decomposeRows}(z)_u). \end{equation} \begin{equation} z = \sum_{v} \varphi_0(\mathrm{decomposeColumns}(z)_v)\cdot \varphi_1(\beta_v). \end{equation} for all $z \in A$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A ring-switching profile: a 2^kappa B-basis of L, an L-algebra carrier A, two homs L to A and row/column coordinate maps obeying two reconstruction laws.
nodes.label: def:ring_switching_profile

nodes.name: Row reconstruction law
nodes.statement: z = \sum_{u} \varphi_0(\beta_u)\cdot \varphi_1(\mathrm{decomposeRows}(z)_u).
nodes.label: eq:rs-rows

nodes.name: Column reconstruction law
nodes.statement: z = \sum_{v} \varphi_0(\mathrm{decomposeColumns}(z)_v)\cdot \varphi_1(\beta_v).
nodes.label: eq:rs-cols

nodes.name: Reconstruction laws are data-layer only
nodes.statement: Laws \eqref{eq:rs-rows}--\eqref{eq:rs-cols} fix the coordinate convention of \cite[\S2.5]{DP24}. They are data-layer reconstruction laws, not completeness or soundness statements. Protocol correctness additionally needs identities connecting these coordinates to packing, the honest folded element, and the batched multiplier. In a nontrivial carrier the laws exclude an identically zero coordinate map; they do not by themselves establish a valid protocol instance or non-vacuous security theorem.
nodes.statement_short: The reconstruction laws fix coordinates but do not by themselves give completeness or soundness.

nodes.name: Tensor-product profile
nodes.statement: For any fields $B = K$ and $L$ with a chosen degree-$2^\kappa$ extension basis, the profile takes the \emph{tensor carrier} $A := L \otimes_K L$, with $\varphi_0(\alpha) = \alpha \otimes 1$, $\varphi_1(\alpha) = 1 \otimes \alpha$, and the coordinate maps given by the $K$-basis coordinates for the left ($\beta.\mathrm{baseChange}\,L$) and right ($\mathrm{baseChangeRight}\,\beta$) $L$-module structures on $A$, giving columns and rows respectively. Thus $z = \sum_v z_v \otimes \beta_v = \sum_u \beta_u \otimes z_u$. Laws \eqref{eq:rs-rows}--\eqref{eq:rs-cols} hold by \texttt{Basis.sum\_repr} on these bases and are proven in ArkLib. Binius uses this constructor with its binary-tower basis.
nodes.label: def:tensor_product_profile

nodes.name: Hachi construction as a ring-switching profile
nodes.statement: The Hachi construction \cite{NOZ26} is the intended second instance: $L = R_q$ a cyclotomic ring, $A = R_q$ itself, $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, $\varphi_1 = \sigma_{-1}$ (the order-two automorphism), and $\beta = \psi$ from its Theorem~2. Because $R_q$ is not an integral domain, the Schwartz--Zippel soundness statement below does not apply to it; Hachi soundness is a separate argument.

nodes.name: Multilinear packing
nodes.statement: With $\ell = \ell' + \kappa$, a small-field multilinear $t$ in $\ell$ variables is packed into a large-field multilinear $t'$ in $\ell'$ variables by bundling each block of $2^\kappa$ coefficients into one $L$-element: \[ t'(w) \;=\; \sum_{v \in \{0,1\}^\kappa} t(v, w)\,\beta_v, \qquad w \in \{0,1\}^{\ell'}. \]
nodes.label: def:pack_mle

nodes.name: Ring-switching reduction (three phases)
nodes.statement: The full reduction is a sequential composition of three phases, ending in a call to an underlying large-field multilinear IOPCS over $L$. \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Batching} (). The prover sends the folded element $\hat s \in A$. The verifier checks the original claim against its column-decomposition, $s = \sum_v \tilde{\mathrm{eq}}(v, r_{0..\kappa-1})\cdot \mathrm{decomposeColumns}(\hat s)_v$, then sends a batching challenge $r'' \in L^\kappa$, collapsing the $\kappa$ packed coordinates into a single sum-check target $s_0 = \sum_u \tilde{\mathrm{eq}}(u, r'')\cdot \mathrm{decomposeRows}(\hat s)_u$. (Soundness loss $\kappa/\lvert L\rvert$.) \item \textbf{Sum-check} (). A degree-$2$ multilinear sum-check over $L$ on $H = A_{\mathrm{MLE}} \cdot t'$, over $\ell'$ rounds plus a final round, reducing the sum claim to a single evaluation of $t'$ at a random point. (Loss $2/\lvert L\rvert$ per round, $1/\lvert L\rvert$ final.) \item \textbf{Opening}. The residual evaluation claim about $t'$ over $L$ is discharged by the underlying large-field multilinear IOPCS.
nodes.statement_short: Batching (send folded s-hat, check columns, batch rows), a degree-2 sum-check over L, then opening via a large-field IOPCS.

nodes.name: Full ring-switching reduction
nodes.statement: The composition of the batching phase, the core sum-check interaction, and the large-field IOPCS invocation.
nodes.label: def:full_ring_switching

nodes.name: Perfect completeness target
nodes.statement: The full ring-switching oracle reduction is perfectly complete: an honest prover holding a witness in the input relation always produces a transcript accepted into the output relation. The honest prover's folded $\hat s$ must satisfy the verifier's column check through the packing and folded-evaluation identities, in addition to reconstruction law \eqref{eq:rs-cols}. These instance-specific identities remain proof obligations in the generic development.
conclusions: The full ring-switching oracle reduction is perfectly complete: an honest prover holding a witness in the input relation always produces a transcript accepted into the output relation.
nodes.label: thm:ring_switching_completeness

nodes.name: Round-by-round knowledge soundness target
nodes.statement: When $L$ is an integral domain, the full reduction is round-by-round knowledge sound, with the additive error \[ \frac{\kappa}{\lvert L\rvert} \;+\; \sum_{\text{rounds}} \frac{2}{\lvert L\rvert} \;+\; \frac{1}{\lvert L\rvert} \;+\; \varepsilon_{\mathrm{IOPCS}}, \] matching \cite[\S3.1--3.2]{DP24}. The integral-domain hypothesis is exactly the Schwartz--Zippel ingredient (a nonzero degree-$d$ univariate over $L$ has at most $d$ roots).
assumptions: When $L$ is an integral domain
conclusions: the full reduction is round-by-round knowledge sound, with the additive error
nodes.label: thm:ring_switching_soundness

nodes.name: Ring-switching security statements are targets
nodes.statement: The leaf completeness and soundness proofs are in progress. The displayed security statements describe targets, not established end-to-end Binius guarantees. A correct instance requires the packing, folded-evaluation, batching, and final-multiplier identities as well as the data-layer reconstruction laws. The concrete tensor instance and its coordinate regressions do not discharge those full protocol obligations.

nodes.name: Binary Tower Field
nodes.statement: A binary tower field $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ for $\iota \in \mathbb{N}$ is defined inductively as the $\iota$-th field in the sequence of quadratic extensions over the ground field $\mathbb{F}_2$. \begin{itemize} \item $\mathcal{T}_{0} := \mathbb{F}_{2}$ \item $\forall \iota > 0$, $\mathcal{T}_{\iota} := \mathcal{T}_{\iota-1}[X_{\iota-1}] / (X_{\iota-1}^{2}+X_{\iota-2} \cdot X_{\iota-1}+1)$, where we conventionally set $X_{-1} := 1$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:binary_tower_field

nodes.name: Irreducible defining polynomial
nodes.statement: The defining polynomial $X_{\iota-1}^{2}+X_{\iota-2} \cdot X_{\iota-1}+1$ of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is irreducible over $\mathcal{T}_{\iota-1}$ for all $\iota > 0$.
conclusions: The defining polynomial $X_{\iota-1}^{2}+X_{\iota-2} \cdot X_{\iota-1}+1$ of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is irreducible over $\mathcal{T}_{\iota-1}$ for all $\iota > 0$.
nodes.label: thm:binary_tower_field_irreducible

nodes.name: Binary Tower Fields are fields
nodes.statement: We prove that the binary tower fields are finite fields: \begin{itemize} \item The ground field $\mathcal{T}_{0} := \mathbb{F}_2$ is a field. For all $\iota > 0$, $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is the quotient ring of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota-1}[X_{\iota-1}]$ by the irreducible polynomial $X_{\iota-1}^{2}+X_{\iota-2} \cdot X_{\iota-1}+1$, therefore $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is a field extension of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota-1}$. \item For all $\iota \in \mathbb{N}$, the cardinality of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is $2^{2^{\iota}}$. \item For all $\iota \in \mathbb{N}$, the characteristic of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is 2. \end{itemize}
conclusions: $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is a field extension of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota-1}$
For all $\iota \in \mathbb{N}$, the cardinality of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is $2^{2^{\iota}}$.
For all $\iota \in \mathbb{N}$, the characteristic of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota}$ is 2.
nodes.label: thm:binary_tower_fields_are_fields

nodes.name: Multilinear Bases for Tower Fields
nodes.statement: For any tower field $\mathcal{T}_\iota$, we define its canonical bases as follows: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{$\mathbb{F}_2$-Basis of $\mathcal{T}_\iota$}: The set of multilinear monomials in the variables $\{X_0, \dots, X_{\iota-1}\}$ forms a basis for $\mathcal{T}_\iota$ as a $2^\iota$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. An element is typically stored as a $2^\iota$-bit string corresponding to this basis. \item \textbf{$\mathcal{T}_\iota$-Basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\iota+\kappa}$}: For any $\kappa \ge 0$, the set of multilinear monomials in the variables $\{X_\iota, \dots, X_{\iota+\kappa-1}\}$ forms a basis for $\mathcal{T}_{\iota+\kappa}$ as a $2^\kappa$-dimensional vector space over the subfield $\mathcal{T}_\iota$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:multilinear_basis

nodes.name: Computable Binary Tower Fields
nodes.statement: Building upon the abstract definition of binary tower fields, we define a concrete, computable representation of binary tower fields. This construction, which underpins our formalization, represents each element of the field $\mathcal{T}_\iota$ as a bit vector of length $2^\iota$ corresponding to the coefficients of the multilinear $\mathbb{F}_2$-basis. The arithmetic operations on these bit-vector representations are defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Addition}: The sum of two elements is defined as the bitwise XOR of their corresponding bit-vector representations. \item \textbf{Multiplication (in $\mathcal{T}_\iota$)}: The product of two elements within the same field $\mathcal{T}_\iota$ is defined via a recursive Karatsuba-based algorithm~\cite{FP97}. The complexity of this operation is $\Theta(2^{\log_2(3) \cdot \iota})$. \item \textbf{Cross-Level Multiplication}: The product of an element $\alpha \in \mathcal{T}_{\iota+\kappa}$ by a scalar $b \in \mathcal{T}_\iota$ is defined by representing $\alpha$ via its $2^\kappa$ coefficients $(a_u)_{u \in \{0,1\}^\kappa}$ in the $\mathcal{T}_\iota$-basis and performing the multiplication component-wise on those coefficients in the subfield $\mathcal{T}_\iota$. The total complexity is $2^\kappa \cdot \Theta(2^{\log_2(3) \cdot \iota})$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Tower field elements as 2^iota-bit vectors: XOR addition, recursive Karatsuba multiplication, component-wise cross-level scalar multiplication.
nodes.label: def:computable_binary_tower_field

nodes.name: Rank-1 Constraint System (R1CS)
nodes.statement: An R1CS instance is defined by a set of matrices $(A, B, C)$ over a field $\mathbb{F}$ (more generally the definition makes sense over any semiring $\mathsf{R}$), and it is satisfied by a public input $x$ and a private witness $w$ if the combined vector $z = (x, w)$ satisfies the relation: \[ (A \cdot z) \circ (B \cdot z) = (C \cdot z) \] where $\circ$ denotes the Hadamard (entry-wise) product.

nodes.name: Spartan PIOP
nodes.statement: After stripping away the polynomial commitment scheme, the protocol has the following structure: \begin{description} \item[Setup:] This step is part of the polynomial commitment scheme and is not part of the PIOP we formalize. \item[Interaction:] The interaction is between a prover $\mathcal{P}$ with witness $w$ and a verifier $\mathcal{V}$ with public inputs $(\mathbb{F}, A, B, C, \text{io}, m, n)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{P}$: Sends oracle access to the multilinear extension of the witness, $\tilde{w}$, to $\mathcal{V}$. In the original paper, this is a commitment $(C,S) \leftarrow \text{PC.Commit}(\text{pp}, \tilde{w})$. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Samples a random challenge $\tau \in \mathbb{F}^{\log m}$ and sends it to $\mathcal{P}$. \item Let $T_1 = 0$, $\mu_1 = \log m$, $\ell_1 = 3$. These are parameters for the first sum-check protocol. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Samples a random challenge $r_x \in \mathbb{F}^{\mu_1}$. \item \textbf{Sum-check\#1.} A sum-check protocol is executed. The verifier receives the claimed evaluation $e_x$. The prover of the sum-check has oracle access to a polynomial $G_{io, \tau}$, and the verifier has oracle access to $r_x$. The parameters for this sub-protocol are $(\mu_1, \ell_1, T_1)$. \item $\mathcal{P}$: Computes evaluations $v_A = \tilde{A}(r_x)$, $v_B = \tilde{B}(r_x)$, $v_C = \tilde{C}(r_x)$ and sends them to $\mathcal{V}$. $\tilde{A}, \tilde{B}, \tilde{C}$ are multilinear extensions of the matrices $A, B, C$. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Aborts if $e_x \neq (v_A \cdot v_B - v_C) \cdot \tilde{\text{eq}}(r_x, \tau)$. This is the verifier's check for the first sum-check. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Samples random challenges $r_A, r_B, r_C \in \mathbb{F}$ and sends them to $\mathcal{P}$. \item Let $T_2 = r_A \cdot v_A + r_B \cdot v_B + r_C \cdot v_C$, $\mu_2 = \log n$, $\ell_2 = 2$. These are parameters for the second sum-check protocol. Note: The image states $\mu_2 = \log m$, which is likely a typo and should be $\log n$. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Samples a random challenge $r_y \in \mathbb{F}^{\mu_2}$. \item \textbf{Sum-check\#2.} Another sum-check protocol is executed. The verifier receives the claimed evaluation $e_y$. \item $\mathcal{P}$: Computes $v \leftarrow \tilde{w}(r_y[1..])$ and sends $v$ to $\mathcal{V}$. \item This step involves a polynomial commitment evaluation proof. In our PIOP formalization, this check is not needed as the verifier has direct oracle access to $\tilde{w}$. \item $\mathcal{V}$: This step is part of the evaluation proof check, so it is omitted. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Computes $v_Z \leftarrow (1 - r_y[0]) \cdot \tilde{w}(r_y[1..]) + r_y[0] \cdot \widetilde{(\text{io}, 1)}(r_y[1..])$. This reconstructs the evaluation of the combined input-witness vector polynomial $\tilde{z}$. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Queries oracles for $\tilde{A}, \tilde{B}, \tilde{C}$ at $(r_x, r_y)$ to get $v_1, v_2, v_3$. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Aborts if $e_y \neq (r_A \cdot v_1 + r_B \cdot v_2 + r_C \cdot v_3) \cdot v_Z$. This is the final check. \item $\mathcal{V}$: Outputs 1.
nodes.statement_short: Spartan PIOP: oracle to the witness MLE, sum-check #1 on the R1CS polynomial, matrix evaluations, sum-check #2, and final checks. Key step: two chained sum-checks.

nodes.name: Proximity gap for Reed-Solomon codes (random linear combination)
nodes.statement: Let $\code := \rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ be a Reed Solomon code with rate $\rate:=\frac{\degree}{|\evaldomain|}$ and let $B^*(\rate):=\sqrt{\rate}$. For every $\distance \in (0,1 - B^*(\rate))$ and functions $f_0,\ldots,f_{m-1} : \evaldomain \to \field$, if \[ \Pr_{r\leftarrow\field}\!\Bigl[ \Delta\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{m-1} r^j\cdot {f_j},\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]\Bigr) \le \delta \Bigr]>\err^*(\degree,\rate,\distance,m), \] then there exists a subset $S \subseteq \evaldomain$ with $|S| \ge (1 - \delta)\cdot|L|$, and for every $i \in [m]$, there exists $u \in \rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ such that $f_i(S) = u(S)$. \medskip \noindent Above, $\err^*(\degree,\rate,\distance,m)$ is defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item if $\distance \in \left(0,\frac{1-\rate}{2}\right]$ then \[ \err^*(\degree,\rate,\distance,m)=\frac{(m-1)\cdot \degree}{\rate\cdot|\field|} \] \item if $\distance \in \Bigl(\frac{1-\rate}{2}, 1-\sqrt{\rate}\Bigr)$ then \[ \err^*(\degree,\rate,\distance,m)=\frac{(m-1)\cdot {\degree}^2}{|\field|\cdot{\Bigl(2\cdot\min\{1-\sqrt{\rate}-\distance,\frac{\sqrt{\rate}}{20}\}\Bigr)}^7} \] \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3.6.1.1 Random linear combination as a proximity generator
assumptions: $\code := \rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ be a Reed Solomon code with rate $\rate:=\frac{\degree}{|\evaldomain|}$
conclusions: there exists a subset $S \subseteq \evaldomain$ with $|S| \ge (1 - \delta)\cdot|L|$, and for every $i \in [m]$, there exists $u \in \rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ such that $f_i(S) = u(S)$
nodes.statement_short: If random linear combinations of f_i are delta-close to RS with probability above err*, then all f_i agree with codewords on a common large set.
nodes.label: thm:proximity_gap

nodes.name: Quotient function
nodes.statement: Let $f:\evaldomain\to\field$ be a function, $S\subseteq\field$ be a set, and $\mathsf{Ans},\mathsf{Fill}: S\rightarrow\field$ be functions. Let $\hat{\mathsf{Ans}}\in\field^{<|S|}[X]$ be the (unique) polynomial with $\hat{\mathsf{Ans}}(x)=\mathsf{Ans}(x)$ for every $x\in S$, and let $\hat{V}_S\in\field^{<|S|+1}[X]$ be the unique non-zero polynomial with $\hat{V}_S(x)=0$ for every $x\in S$. The \emph{quotient function} $\mathsf{Quotient}\bigl(f,S,\mathsf{Ans},\mathsf{Fill}\bigr): \evaldomain\to\field$ is defined as follows: \[ \forall x \in \evaldomain, \quad \mathsf{Quotient}\bigl(f, S, \mathsf{Ans}, \mathsf{Fill} \bigr)(x) := \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \mathsf{Fill}(x) & \text{if } x \in S \\[6pt] \dfrac{f(x) - \hat{\mathsf{Ans}}(x)}{\hat{V}_S(x)} & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \]
nodes.label: def:quotient

nodes.name: Polynomial quotient
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{f}\in\field^{<\degree}[X]$ be a polynomial and $S\subseteq\field$ be a set, let $\hat{V}_S\in\field^{<|S|+1}[X]$ be the unique non-zero polynomial with $\hat{V}_S(x)=0$ for every $x\in S$. The \emph{polynomial quotient} $\mathsf{PolyQuotient}(\hat{f},S)\in\field^{<d-|S|}[X]$ is defined as follows: \[ \mathsf{PolyQuotient}(\hat{f},S)(X):=\frac{\hat{f}(X)-\hat{\mathsf{Ans}}(X)}{\hat{V}_S(X)} \] where $\hat{Ans}\in\field^{<|S|}[X]$ is the unique non-zero polynomial with $\hat{Ans}(x)=\hat{f}(x)$ for every $x \in S$.
nodes.label: def:poly_quotient

nodes.name: Quotienting lemma
nodes.statement: Let $f:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ be a function, $\degree\in\N$ be the degree parameter, $\distance\in(0,1)$ be a distance parameter, $S\subseteq\field$ be a set with $|S|<\degree$, and $\mathsf{Ans},\mathsf{Fill}:S\rightarrow\field$ are functions. Suppose that for every $u\in\listcode(f,\degree,\distance)$ there exists $x\in S$ with $\hat{u}(x)\neq\mathsf{Ans}(x)$. Then \[ \Delta(\mathsf{Quotient}(f,S,\mathsf{Ans},\mathsf{Fill}),\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree-|S|])+\frac{|T|}{|\evaldomain|}>\distance, \] where $T:=\{x\in\evaldomain\cap S: \hat{\mathsf{Ans}}(x)\neq f(x)\}$.
assumptions: Suppose that for every $u\in\listcode(f,\degree,\distance)$ there exists $x\in S$ with $\hat{u}(x)\neq\mathsf{Ans}(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotienting by wrong answers yields a function far from the lower-degree RS code.
nodes.label: lemma:quotienting

nodes.name: Out-of-domain sampling lemma
nodes.statement: Let $f:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ be a function, $\degree\in\N$ be a degree parameter, $s\in\N$ be a repetition parameter, and $\distance\in[0,1]$ be a distance parameter. If $\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ be $(\degree,l)$-list decodable then \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \Pr_{\substack{r_0, \ldots, r_{s-1} \gets \field \setminus \evaldomain}} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \exists \text{ distinct } u, u' \in \listcode(f, \degree, \distance): \\ \forall i \in [s],\ \hat{u}(r_i) = \hat{u}'(r_i) \end{array} \right] & \leq & \binom{l}{2} \cdot \left( \frac{\degree - 1}{|\field| - |\evaldomain|} \right)^s \\ & \leq & \left( \frac{l^2}{2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\degree}{|\field| - |\evaldomain|} \right)^s \end{array} \]
assumptions: If $\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ be $(\degree,l)$-list decodable
nodes.statement_short: Out-of-domain samples distinguish list-decoded codewords except with probability about (l^2/2)(d/(|F|-|L|))^s.
nodes.label: lemma:out_of_domain_smpl

nodes.name: Polynomial folding decomposition
nodes.statement: Given a polynomial $\hat{q}\in\field[X]$: \begin{itemize} \item For every univariate polynomial $\hat{f}\in\field[X]$, there exists a unique bivariate polynomial $\hat{Q}\in\field[X,Y]$ with: \[ \polydeg_X(\hat{Q}) := \left\lfloor \frac{\polydeg(\hat{f})}{\polydeg(\hat{q})} \right\rfloor,\quad \polydeg_Y(\hat{Q}) < \polydeg(\hat{q}) \] such that $\hat{f}(Z)=\hat{Q}(\hat{q}(Z),Z)$. Moreover, $\hat{Q}$ can be computed efficiently given $\hat{f}$ and $\hat{q}$. Observe that if $\polydeg(\hat{f})<t\cdot\polydeg(\hat{q})$ then $\polydeg(\hat{Q})<t$. \item For every $\hat{Q}[X,Y]$ with $\polydeg_X(\hat{Q})<t$ and $\polydeg_Y(\hat{Q})<\polydeg(\hat{q})$, the polynomial $\hat{f}(Z)=\hat{Q}(\hat{q}(Z),Z)$ has degree $\polydeg(\hat{f})<t\cdot\polydeg(\hat{q})$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Every univariate f decomposes uniquely as Q(q(Z), Z) with bounded bivariate degrees, and conversely.
nodes.label: fact:poly_folding

nodes.name: Polynomial folding
nodes.statement: Given a polynomial $\hat{f}\in\field^{<\degree}[X]$, a folding parameter $k\in\N$ and $r\in\field$, we define a polynomial $\mathsf{PolyFold}(\hat{f},k,r)\in\field^{\degree/k}[X]$ as follows. Let $\hat{Q}[X,Y]$ be the bivariate polynomial derived from $\hat{f}$ using Fact~\ref{fact:poly_folding} with $\hat{q}(X):=X^k$. Then $\mathsf{PolyFold}(\hat{f},k,r)(X):=\hat{Q}(X,r)$.
nodes.label: def:poly_folding

nodes.name: Function folding
nodes.statement: Let $f:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ be a function, $k\in\N$ a folding parameter and $\alpha\in\field$. For every $x\in{\evaldomain}^k$, let $\hat{p}_x\in\field^{<k}[X]$ be the polynomial where $\hat{p}_x(y)=f(y)$ for every $y\in{\evaldomain}$ such that $y^k=x$. We define $\mathsf{Fold}(f,k,\alpha):\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ as follows. \[ \mathsf{Fold}(f,k,\alpha):=\hat{p}_x(\alpha). \] In order to compute $\mathsf{Fold}(f,k,\alpha)(x)$ it suffices to interpolate the $k$ values $\{f(y):y\in\evaldomain\text{ s.t. }y^k=x\}$ into the polynomial $\hat{p}_x$ and evaluate this polynomial at $\alpha$.
nodes.label: def:fn_folding

nodes.name: Folding preserves distance
nodes.statement: For every function $f:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$, degree parameter $\degree\in\N$, folding parameter $k\in\N$, distance parameter $\distance\in(0,\min\{{\Delta(\mathsf{Fold}[f,k,r^{\mathsf{fold}}],\rscode[\field,{\evaldomain}^k, \degree/k]),1-{\mathsf{B}}^*(\rate)}\})$, letting $\rate:=\frac{\degree}{|\evaldomain|}$, \[ \Pr_{r^{\mathsf{fold}}\gets\field}[\Delta(\mathsf{Fold}[f,k,r^{\mathsf{fold}}],\rscode[\field,{\evaldomain}^k, \degree/k])<\distance]>\err^*(\degree/k,\rate,\distance,k). \] Above, ${\mathsf{B}}^*$ and ${\err}^*$ are the proximity bound and error (respectively) described in Section~\ref{sec:proximity_gap}.
nodes.statement_short: With high probability over folding randomness, k-wise folding preserves distance from the RS code.
nodes.label: lemma:folding

nodes.name: Geometric sum formula
nodes.statement: Let $\field$ be a field, $r\in\field$ be a field element, $a\in\N$ be a natural number. Then \[ \sum_{i=0}^{a} r^i := \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle\left(\frac{1 - r^{a+1}}{1 - r}\right) & \text{if } r \neq 1 \\[6pt] a + 1 & \text{if } r = 1 \end{array} \right. \]
nodes.label: fact:geometric_sum

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Given target degree $\degree^*\in\N$, shifting parameter $r\in\field$, functions $f_0,\ldots,f_{m-1}:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$, and degrees $0\leq \degree_0,\ldots,\degree_{m-1}\leq {\degree}^*$, we define $\combine(\degree^*,r,(f_0,\degree_0),\ldots,(f_{m-1},\degree_{m-1})):\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ as follows: \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \combine(\degree^*, r, (f_0, \degree_0), \ldots, (f_{m-1}, \degree_{m-1}))(x) & := & \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} r_i \cdot f_i(x) \cdot \left( \sum_{l=0}^{\degree^* - \degree_i} (r \cdot x)^l \right) \\[10pt] & = & \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} r_i \cdot f_i(x) \cdot \left( \dfrac{1 - (x r)^{\degree^* - \degree_i + 1}}{1 - x r} \right) & \text{if } x \cdot r \neq 1 \\[8pt] \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} r_i \cdot f_i(x) \cdot (\degree^* - \degree_i + 1) & \text{if } x \cdot r = 1 \end{array} \right. \end{array} \] Above, $r_i:=r^{i-1+\sum_{j<i}(\degree^*-\degree_j)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine functions of varying degrees into one target-degree function using powers of r and geometric-sum degree correction.
nodes.label: def:combine

nodes.name: Degree correction
nodes.statement: Given target degree $\degree^*\in\N$, shifting parameter $r\in\field$, function $f:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$, and degree $0\leq\degree\leq\degree^*$, we define $\degcorr(\degree^*,r,f,\degree)$ as follows. \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \degcorr(\degree^*, r, f, \degree)(x) & := & \displaystyle f(x) \cdot \left( \sum_{l=0}^{\degree^* - \degree} (r \cdot x)^l \right) \\[10pt] & = & \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle f(x) \cdot \left( \dfrac{1 - (x r)^{\degree^* - \degree_i + 1}}{1 - x r} \right) & \text{if } x \cdot r \neq 1 \\[8pt] \displaystyle f(x) \cdot (\degree^* - \degree_i + 1) & \text{if } x \cdot r = 1 \end{array} \right. \end{array} \] (Observe that $\degcorr(\degree^*,r,f,\degree)=\combine(\degree^*,r,(f,\degree))$.)
nodes.label: def:deg_corr

nodes.name: Combine lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\degree^*$ be a target degree, $f_0,\ldots,f_{m-1}:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ be functions, $0\leq \degree_0,\ldots,\degree_{m-1}\leq \degree^*$ be degrees, $\distance\in\min{\{1-{\mathsf{B}}^*(\rate),1-\rate-1/|\evaldomain|\}}$ be a distance parameter, where $\rate=\degree^*/|\evaldomain|$. If \[ \Pr_{r\gets\field}[\Delta(\combine(\degree^*,r,(f_0,\degree_0),\ldots,(f_{m-1},\degree_{m-1})),\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree^*])]>\err^*(\degree^*,\rate,\distance,m\cdot(\degree^*+1)-\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\degree_i), \] then there exists $S\subseteq \evaldomain$ with $|S|\geq(1-\distance)\cdot|\evaldomain|$, and \[ \forall i\in[m-1],\exists u\in\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree_i], f_i(S)=u(S). \] Note that this implies $\Delta(f_i,\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree_i])<\distance$ for every $i$. Above, ${\mathsf{B}}^*$ and ${\err}^*$ are the proximity bound and error (respectively) described in the proximity gap theorem.
conclusions: there exists $S\subseteq \evaldomain$ with $|S|\geq(1-\distance)\cdot|\evaldomain|$
nodes.statement_short: If the combination is close to RS with high probability, each f_i agrees with a degree-d_i codeword on a common large set.
nodes.label: lemma:combine

nodes.name: STIR Main Theorem
nodes.statement: Consider the following ingrediants: \begin{itemize} \item A security parameter $\lambda\in\N$. \item A Reed-Solomon code $\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ with $\rate:=\frac{\degree}{|\evaldomain|}$ where $\degree$ is a power of $2$, and $\evaldomain$ is a smooth domain. \item A proximity parameter $\distance\in(0,1-1.05\cdot\sqrt{\rate})$. \item A folding parameter $k\in\N$ that is power of $2$ with $k\geq 4$. \end{itemize} If $|\field|=\Omega(\frac{\lambda\cdot2^\lambda\cdot\degree^2\cdot{|\evaldomain|}^2}{\log(1/\rate)})$, there is a public-coin IOPP for $\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ with the following parameters: \begin{itemize} \item Round-by-round soundness error $2^{-\lambda}$. \item Round complexity: $M:=O(\log_k{\degree})$. \item Proof length: $|\evaldomain|+O_k(\log{\degree})$. \item Query complexity to the input: $\frac{\lambda}{-\log{(1-\distance)}}$. \item Query complexity to the proof strings: $O_k(\log{\degree}+\lambda\cdot\log{\Big(\frac{\log{\degree}}{\log{1/\rate}}\Big)})$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: there is a public-coin IOPP for $\rscode[\field,\evaldomain,\degree]$ with the following parameters:
nodes.statement_short: STIR: an IOPP for RS codes with RBR soundness 2^-lambda, O(log_k d) rounds and query complexity logarithmic in degree.
nodes.label: thm:stir

nodes.name: STIR round-by-round soundness
nodes.statement: Consider $(\field,M,\degree,k_0,\ldots,k_M,\evaldomain_0,\ldots,\evaldomain_M,t_0,\ldots,t_M)$ and for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,M\}$, let $\degree_i:=\frac{\degree}{\prod_{j<i}k^j}$ and $\rate_i:=\degree_i/|\evaldomain_i|$. For every $f\notin\rscode[\field,\evaldomain_0,\degree_0]$ and every $\distance_0,\ldots,\distance_M$ where \begin{itemize} \item $\distance_0\in(0,\Delta(f,\rscode[\field,\evaldomain_0,\degree_0])]\cap(0,1-{\mathsf{B}}^*(\rate_0))$ \item for every $0<i\leq M$: $\distance_i\in(0,\min{\{1-\rate_i-\frac{1}{|\evaldomain_i|},1-{\mathsf{B}^*(\rate_i)}\}})$, and \item for every $0<i\leq M$: $\rscode[\field,\evaldomain_i,\degree_i]$ is $(\distance_i,l_i)$-list decodable, \end{itemize} There exists an IOPP with above parameters, that has round-by-round soundness error $(\epsilon^{\mathsf{fold}},\epsilon^{\mathsf{out}}_1,\epsilon^{\mathsf{shift}}_1,\ldots,\epsilon^{\mathsf{out}}_M,\epsilon^{\mathsf{shift}}_M,\epsilon^{\mathsf{fin}})$ where: \begin{itemize} \item $\epsilon^{\mathsf{fold}}\leq\err^*(\degree_0/k_0,\rate_0,\distance_0,k_0)$. \item $\epsilon^{\mathsf{out}}_i\leq\frac{l^2_i}{2}\cdot{\big(\frac{\degree_i}{|\field|-|\evaldomain_i|}\big)}^s$ \item $\epsilon^{\mathsf{shift}}_i\leq {(1-\distance_{i-1})}^{t_{i-1}}+\err^*(\degree_i,\rate_i,\distance_i,t_{i-1}+s)+\err^*(\degree_i/k_i,\rate_i,\distance_i,k_i)$. \item $\epsilon^{\mathsf{fin}}\leq{(1-\distance_M)}^{t_M}$. \end{itemize} Above, ${\mathsf{B}}^*$ and ${\err}^*$ are the proximity bound and error (respectively) described in Section~\ref{sec:proximity_gap}.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit round-by-round soundness errors for STIR folding, out-of-domain, shift and final rounds.
nodes.label: lemma:rnd_by_rnd_soundness

nodes.name: Proximity generator
nodes.statement: Let $\code\subseteq \field^{\evaldomain}$ be a linear code. We say that $\mathsf{Gen}$ is a proximity generator for $\code$ with proximity bounds ${\bound}$ and $\err$ if the following implication holds for $f_0,\ldots,f_{\parl-1} : \evaldomain \rightarrow \field$ and $\delta\in(0,1-{\bound}(\rate,\parl))$. If \begin{align*} \Pr_{r_0,\ldots,r_{\parl-1}\leftarrow \gen}[\Delta(\sum_{i\in[0,(\parl-1)]} r_i \cdot f_i, \code) \le \delta] > err(\code,\parl,\delta), \end{align*} then there exists $S\subseteq \evaldomain$, $|S|>(1-\delta)\cdot|\evaldomain|$, and $\forall i \in [0, (\parl-1)]$, $\exists u \in \code, \forall x \in S$, $f_i(x)=u(x)$.
nodes.section: 3.7.1.1 Mutual Correlated Agreement as a Proximity Generator
nodes.label: def:proximity_generator

nodes.name: Proximity gap for Reed-Solomon codes (WHIR)
nodes.statement: Let $\code = \rscode[\field,\evaldomain,m]$ be a Reed Solomon code with rate $\rate = 2^m/|\evaldomain|$. $\gen(\alpha,\parl)=\{1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{\parl-1}\}$ is a proximity generator for $\code$ with proximity bounds ${\bound}(\rate,\parl)=\sqrt{\rate}$ and $\err(C,\parl,\delta)$ defined below. \begin{itemize} \item if $\distance \in \left(0,\frac{1-\rate}{2}\right]$ then \[ \err(\code,\parl,\delta)=\frac{(m-1)\cdot \degree}{\rate\cdot|\field|} \] \item if $\distance \in \Bigl(\frac{1-\rate}{2}, 1-\sqrt{\rate}\Bigr)$ then \[ \err(\code,\parl,\delta)=\frac{(m-1)\cdot {\degree}^2}{|\field|\cdot{\Bigl(2\cdot\min\{1-\sqrt{\rate}-\distance,\frac{\sqrt{\rate}}{20}\}\Bigr)}^7} \] \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3.7.1.1 Mutual Correlated Agreement as a Proximity Generator
conclusions: $\gen(\alpha,\parl)=\{1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{\parl-1}\}$ is a proximity generator for $\code$ with proximity bounds ${\bound}(\rate,\parl)=\sqrt{\rate}$
nodes.label: thm:proximity_gap_whir

nodes.name: Mutual correlated agreement
nodes.statement: Let $\code$ be a linear code. We say that $\gen$ be a proximity generator with mutual correlated agreement with proximity bounds ${\bound}^\star$ and $\err^\star$, if for $f_0,\ldots,f_{\parl-1}:\evaldomain\rightarrow\field$ and $\delta\in(0,1-{\bound}^\star(\code,\parl))$ the following holds. \[ \Pr_{(r_0, \ldots, r_{\parl-1}) \leftarrow \gen(\parl)} \left[ \exists S \subseteq \evaldomain \;\; s.t.\;\; \begin{array}{l} |S| \geq (1 - \delta) \cdot |\evaldomain| \\ \land\; \exists u \in \code, u(S) = \sum_{j \in [0,(\parl-1)]} r_j \cdot f_j(S) \\ \land\; \exists i \in [0,(\parl-1)], \forall u' \in \code, u'(S) \neq f_i(S) \end{array}\right] \leq \err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta). \]
nodes.section: 3.7.1.1 Mutual Correlated Agreement as a Proximity Generator
nodes.definiendum: proximity generator with mutual correlated agreement
nodes.label: def:gen_mutual_corr_agreement

nodes.name: Proximity generators have mutual correlated agreement
nodes.statement: Let $\code$ be a linear code with minimum distance $\delta_{\code}$ and let $\gen$ be a proximity generator for $\code$ with proximity bound ${\bound}$ and error $\err$. Then $\gen$ has mutual correlated agreement with proximity bound ${\bound}^\star(\code, \parl) = \min\{1 - \delta_{\code}/2, \bound(\code, \parl)\}$ and error $\err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta) := \err(\code, \parl, \delta)$.
nodes.section: 3.7.1.1 Mutual Correlated Agreement as a Proximity Generator
assumptions: $\code$ be a linear code with minimum distance $\delta_{\code}$
let $\gen$ be a proximity generator for $\code$ with proximity bound ${\bound}$ and error $\err$
conclusions: $\gen$ has mutual correlated agreement with proximity bound ${\bound}^\star(\code, \parl) = \min\{1 - \delta_{\code}/2, \bound(\code, \parl)\}$ and error $\err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta) := \err(\code, \parl, \delta)$
nodes.label: lemma:gen_mutual_corr_agreement

nodes.name: Mutual correlated agreement for Reed-Solomon codes (unique decoding)
nodes.statement: Let $\code := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ be a Reed Solomon code with rate $\rate$. The function $\gen(\parl; \alpha) = (1, \alpha, \ldots, \alpha^{\parl - 1})$ is a proximity generator for $\code$ with mutual correlated agreement with proximity bound ${\bound}^\star(\code, \parl) := \frac{1 + \rate}{2}$ and error $\err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta) = \frac{(\parl - 1) \cdot 2^m}{\rate \cdot |\field|}$.
nodes.section: 3.7.1.1 Mutual Correlated Agreement as a Proximity Generator
assumptions: $\code := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ be a Reed Solomon code with rate $\rate$
conclusions: The function $\gen(\parl; \alpha) = (1, \alpha, \ldots, \alpha^{\parl - 1})$ is a proximity generator for $\code$ with mutual correlated agreement with proximity bound ${\bound}^\star(\code, \parl) := \frac{1 + \rate}{2}$ and error $\err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta) = \frac{(\parl - 1) \cdot 2^m}{\rate \cdot |\field|}$

nodes.name: WHIR mutual correlated agreement conjecture
nodes.statement: The function $\gen(\parl; \alpha) := (1, \alpha, \ldots, \alpha^{\parl - 1})$ is a proximity generator with mutual correlated agreement for every smooth Reed Solomon code $\code := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ (with rate $\rate := 2^m / |\evaldomain|$). We give two conjectures, for the parameters of the proximity bound ${\bound}^\star$ and the error $\err^\star$: \begin{enumerate} \item \textit{Up to the Johnson bound:} ${\bound}^\star(\code, \parl) := \sqrt{\rate},$ \textit{and} \[ \err(\code, \parl, \delta) := \frac{(\parl - 1) \cdot 2^m}{|\field| \cdot \left( 2 \cdot \min\left\{1 - \sqrt{\rate} - \delta, \frac{\sqrt{\rate}}{20} \right\} \right)^7}. \] \item \textit{Up to capacity:} ${\bound}^\star(\code, \parl) := \rate$, \textit{and there exist constants $c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $\eta > 0$ and $0 < \delta < 1 - \rate - \eta$:} \[ \err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta) := \frac{(\parl - 1)^{c_2} \cdot \delta^{c_2}}{\eta^{c_1} \cdot \rate^{c_1 + c_2} \cdot |\field|}. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.7.1.1 Mutual Correlated Agreement as a Proximity Generator
nodes.statement_short: Conjecture: powers-of-alpha generators have mutual correlated agreement up to the Johnson bound, or even up to capacity.
nodes.label: conjecture:whir

nodes.name: Mutual correlated agreement preserves list decoding
nodes.statement: Let $\code \subseteq \field^{\evaldomain}$ be a linear code with minimum distance $\delta_{\code}$, and let $\gen$ be a proximity generator for $\code$ with mutual correlated agreement with proximity bound ${\bound}^\star$ and error $\err^\star$. Then, for every $f_0, \ldots, f_{\parl-1} : \evaldomain \to \field$ and $\delta \in (0, \min\{\delta_{\code}, 1 - {\bound}^\star(\code, \parl)\})$: \[ \Pr_{\substack{\alpha \leftarrow \{0,1\}^{w^\star} \\ \boldsymbol{r} := \gen(\parl; \alpha)}} \left[ \Lambda\left(\code, \sum_{j \in [0,(\parl-1)]} r_j \cdot f_j, \delta \right) \neq \left\{ \sum_{j \in [0,(\parl-1)]} r_j \cdot u_j : \boldsymbol{u} \in \Lambda\left(\mathcal{C}^\ell, (f_0, \ldots, f_{\parl-1}), \delta \right) \right\} \right] \leq \err^\star(\code, \parl, \delta). \]
nodes.section: 3.7.1.2 Mutual correlated agreement preserves list decoding
nodes.label: lemma: mutual_corrAgr_listdecoding

nodes.name: Extract
nodes.statement: Let $\mathsf{extract}:\evaldomain^{2^{k+1}}\rightarrow \evaldomain^{2^k}$ be a function. There exists $x \in \evaldomain$, such that $y = x^{2^{k+1}}\in\evaldomain^{2^{k+1}}$. Then $\mathsf{extract}$ returns $z = \sqrt{y} = x^{2^k}\in\evaldomain^{2^k}$ such that $y = z^2$.
nodes.label: def:extract

nodes.name: Single fold
nodes.statement: Let $f : \evaldomain^{2^k} \to \field$ be a function, and $\alpha \in \field$. We define $\mathrm{Fold_f}(f, {\alpha}) : \evaldomain^{(2^{k+1})} \to \field$ as follows: \[ \forall x \in \evaldomain^{2^k}, y \in \evaldomain^{2^{k+1}}, \quad \mathrm{Fold_f}(f, \alpha)(y) := \frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2} + \alpha \cdot \frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2 \cdot x}. \] In order to compute $\mathrm{Fold_f}(f, \alpha)(y)$ it suffices to query $f$ at $x$ and $-x$, by retrieving $x=\mathsf{extract}(y)$.
nodes.label: def:foldf

nodes.name: k-wise fold
nodes.statement: For $k \leq m$ and $\vec{\alpha} = (\alpha_0, \ldots, \alpha_{k-1}) \in \field^k$ we define $\mathrm{Fold}(f, \vec{\alpha}) : \evaldomain^{2^k} \to \field$ to equal $\mathrm{Fold}(f, \vec{\alpha}) := f_k$ where $f_k$ is defined recursively as follows: $f_0 := f$, and $f_i := \mathrm{Fold_f}(f_{i-1}, \alpha_i)$.
nodes.label: def:fold_k

nodes.name: Fold of a set
nodes.statement: For a set $S \subseteq \field^{\evaldomain}$ we denote $\mathrm{Fold_{S}}(S, \vec{\alpha}) := \{\mathrm{Fold_{S}}(f, \vec{\alpha}) \mid f \in S\}$.
nodes.label: def:fold_k_set

nodes.name: Folding Reed-Solomon codewords
nodes.statement: Let $f : \evaldomain \to \field$ be a function, $\vec{\alpha} \in \field^k$ folding randomness and let $g := \mathrm{Fold}(f, \vec{\alpha})$. If $f \in \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ and $k \leq m$, then $g \in \rscode[\field, \evaldomain^{2^k}, m - k]$, and further the multilinear extension of $g$ is given by $\hat{g}(X_k, \ldots, X_{m-1}) := \hat{f}(\vec{\alpha}, X_k, \ldots, X_{m-1})$ where $\hat{f}$ is the multilinear extension of $f$.
assumptions: $f \in \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ and $k \leq m$
conclusions: $g \in \rscode[\field, \evaldomain^{2^k}, m - k]$, and further the multilinear extension of $g$ is given by $\hat{g}(X_k, \ldots, X_{m-1}) := \hat{f}(\vec{\alpha}, X_k, \ldots, X_{m-1})$ where $\hat{f}$ is the multilinear extension of $f$
nodes.label: lemma:fold_fg

nodes.name: Block
nodes.statement: Let $\evaldomain \subseteq \field$ be a smooth evaluation domain and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ be a folding parameter. For $z \in \evaldomain^{2^k}$, define $\mathrm{Block}(\evaldomain, i, k, z) := \{ x \in \evaldomain, y \in \evaldomain^{2^i} : y^{2^{k-i}} = z \}$.
nodes.label: def:block

nodes.name: Block relative distance
nodes.statement: Let $\code := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ be a smooth Reed Solomon code and let $f, g : \evaldomain^{2^i} \to \field$. We define the $(i,k)$-wise block relative distance as \[ \Delta_{r}(\code, i, k, f, g) = \frac{ \left| \left\{ z \in \evaldomain^{2^k} : \exists y \in \mathrm{Block}(\evaldomain, i, k, z), f(y) \neq g(y) \right\} \right| }{ |\evaldomain^{2^k}| } \]
nodes.label: def:block_rel_distance

nodes.name: Block relative distance to a set
nodes.statement: For $S \subseteq \field^{\evaldomain}$, we let $\Delta_{r}(\code, i, k, f, S) := \min_{g \in S} \Delta_{r}(\code, i, k, f, g)$.
nodes.label: def:min_block_rel_distance

nodes.name: Block distance at (0,0) equals Hamming distance
nodes.statement: Note that $\Delta_{r}(\code, 0, 0, f, g) = \Delta(f, g)$ for any $\code$.

nodes.name: Block list decoding
nodes.statement: For a smooth Reed Solomon code $\rscode := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$, proximity parameter $\delta \in [0,1]$, and $f : \evaldomain^{2^i} \to \field$, we let \[ \Lambda_{r}(\code, i, k, f, \delta) := \{ u \in \code \mid \Delta_{r}(\code, i, k, f, u) \leq \delta \}, \] denote the list of codewords in $\code$ within relative block distance at most $\delta$ from $f$.
nodes.label: def:list_close_codewords_block

nodes.name: Block distance bounds distance
nodes.statement: For any $\code := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and $f, g : \evaldomain^{2^i} \to \field$, we have that $\Delta(f, g) \leq \Delta_{r}(\code, i, k, f, g)$. Consequently, $\Lambda_{r}(\code, i, k, f, \delta) \subseteq \Lambda(\code, f, \delta)$ for $\delta\in[0,1]$.
conclusions: $\Delta(f, g) \leq \Delta_{r}(\code, i, k, f, g)$
$\Lambda_{r}(\code, i, k, f, \delta) \subseteq \Lambda(\code, f, \delta)$ for $\delta\in[0,1]$
nodes.label: lemma:block_rel_distance

nodes.name: Folding preserves list decoding
nodes.statement: Let $\code = \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ be a smooth Reed Solomon code and $k \leq m$. For $0 \leq i \leq k$ let $\code^{(i)} := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain^{2^i}, m - i]$. Let $\gen(\parl; \alpha) = (1, \alpha, \ldots, \alpha^{\parl - 1})$ be a proximity generator with mutual correlated agreement for the codes $\code^{(0)}, \ldots, \mathcal{C}^{(k-1)}$ with proximity bound ${\bound}^\star$ and error $\err^\star$. Then for every $f : \evaldomain \to \field$ and $\delta \in \left(0, 1 - \max_{i \in [0,(k-1)]} \{ {\bound}^\star(\code^{(i)}, 2) \} \right)$, \[ \Pr_{\alpha \leftarrow \field^k} \left[ \mathrm{Fold_S}(\Lambda_{r}(\code, 0, k, f, \delta), \alpha) \neq \Lambda(\code^{(k)}, \mathrm{Fold}(f, \alpha), \delta) \right] < \err^{(k)}(\code, \delta). \]
nodes.statement_short: With high probability over alpha, folding the block list of f equals the list of the folded function.
nodes.label: thm:folding_preserves_listdecoding

nodes.name: Folding preserves list decoding (one step)
nodes.statement: Let $\code := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ be a Reed Solomon code, and $k \leq m$ be a parameter. Denote $\code' := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain^{2}, m - 1]$. Then for every $f : \evaldomain \to \field$ and $\delta \in (0, 1 - {\bound}^\star(\code', 2))$, \[ \Pr_{\alpha \leftarrow \field} \left[ \mathrm{Fold_S}(\Lambda_{r}(\code, 0, k, f, \delta), \alpha) \neq \Lambda_{r}(\code', 1, k, \mathrm{Fold}(f, \alpha), \delta) \right] < \err^\star(\code', 2, \delta). \]
nodes.label: lemma:folding_preserves_listdecoding_base

nodes.name: Folding list inclusion
nodes.statement: For every $\alpha \in \field$, $\mathrm{Fold_S}(\Lambda_{r}(\code, 0, k, f, \delta), \alpha) \subseteq \Lambda_{r}(\code', 1, k, \mathrm{Fold}(f, \alpha), \delta)$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{Fold_S}(\Lambda_{r}(\code, 0, k, f, \delta), \alpha) \subseteq \Lambda_{r}(\code', 1, k, \mathrm{Fold}(f, \alpha), \delta)$
nodes.label: lemma:folding_preserves_listdecoding_bound

nodes.name: Folding list reverse inclusion fails rarely
nodes.statement: \[ \Pr_{\alpha \leftarrow \field} \left[ \Lambda_{r}(\code', 1, k, \mathrm{Fold}(f, \alpha), \delta) \not\subseteq \mathrm{Fold_S}(\Lambda_{r}(\code, 0, k, f, \delta), \alpha) \right] < \err^\star(\code', 2, \delta). \]
nodes.label: lemma:folding_preserves_listdecoding_base_ne_subset

nodes.name: Constrained RS list size vs random-point agreement
nodes.statement: Let $f : \evaldomain \rightarrow \field$ be a function, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ be a number of variables, $s \in \mathbb{N}$ be a repetition parameter, and let $\delta \in [0,1]$ be a distance parameter. For every $\vec{r_0}, \dots, \vec{r_{s-1}} \in \field^m$, the following are equivalent statements. \begin{itemize} \item There exist distinct $u, u' \in \Lambda(\rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m], f, \delta)$ such that, for every $i \in [0,s-1]$, $\hat{u}(\vec{r_i}) = \hat{u}'(\vec{r_i})$. \item There exists $\sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_{s-1} \in \field$ such that $$\left| \Lambda(\crscode[\field, \evaldomain, m, ((Z \cdot \mathrm{eq}(\vec{r_0}, \cdot), \sigma_0), \dots, (Z \cdot \mathrm{eq}(\vec{r_{s-1}}, \cdot), \sigma_{s-1}))], f, \delta) \right| > 1.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Two list codewords agreeing on all eq-points iff some constrained RS code has more than one close codeword.
nodes.label: lemma:crs_equiv_rs_randpompt_agreement

nodes.name: Out-of-domain sampling for constrained RS codes
nodes.statement: Let $f : \evaldomain \rightarrow \field$ be a function, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ be a number of variables, $s \in \mathbb{N}$ be a repetition parameter, and $\delta \in [0,1]$ be a distance parameter. If $\rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ is $(\delta, \ell)$-list decodable then \[ \Pr_{r_0, \dots, r_{s-1} \leftarrow \field} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \exists \sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_{s-1} \in \field \text{ s.t.} \\ \left| \Lambda(\crscode[\field, \evaldomain, m, ((Z \cdot \mathrm{eq}(\mathrm{pow}(r_{i}, m), \cdot), \sigma_{i}))_{i \in [s]}], f, \delta) \right| > 1 \end{array} \right] \] \[ = \Pr_{r_0, \dots, r_{s-1} \leftarrow \field} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \exists \text{ distinct } u, u' \in \Lambda(\rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m], f, \delta) \\ \text{ s.t. } \forall i \in [s],\ \hat{u}(\mathrm{pow}(r_i, m)) = \hat{u}'(\mathrm{pow}(r_i, m)) \end{array} \right] \] \[ \leq \frac{\ell^2}{2} \cdot \left( \frac{2^m}{|\field|} \right)^s. \]
assumptions: If $\rscode[\field, \evaldomain, m]$ is $(\delta, \ell)$-list decodable
nodes.label: lemma:out_of_domain_sampling_crs_eq_rs

nodes.name: WHIR round-by-round soundness
nodes.statement: Consider $(\field, M, (k_i, m_i, \evaldomain_i, t_i)_{0 \leq i \leq M}, \widehat{w}_0, \sigma_0, m, d^\star, d)$ with the following ingrediants and conditions, \begin{itemize} \item a constrained Reed Solomon code $\crscode[\field, \evaldomain_0, m_0, \widehat{w}_0, \sigma_0]$; \item an iteration count $M \in \mathbb{N}$; \item folding parameters $k_0, \ldots, k_{M}$ such that $\sum_{i=0}^{M} k_i \leq m$; \item evaluation domains $\evaldomain_0, \ldots, \evaldomain_{M} \subseteq \field$ where $\evaldomain_i$ is a smooth coset of $\field^*$ with order $|\evaldomain_i| \geq 2^{m_i}$; \item repetition parameters $t_0, \ldots, t_M$ with $t_i \leq |\evaldomain_i|$; \item define $m_0 := m$ and $m_i := m - \sum_{j < i} k_j$; \item define $d^\star := 1 + \deg_{\mathbb{Z}}(\widehat{w}_0) + \max_{i \in [m_0]} \deg_{X_i}(\widehat{w}_0)$ and $d := \max\{d^\star, 3\}$. \end{itemize} For every $f \notin \crscode[\field, \evaldomain_0, m_0, \widehat{w}_0, \sigma_0]$ and every $\delta_0, \dots, \delta_{M}$ and $(\parl_{i,s})_{0 \leq i \leq M}^{0 \leq s \leq k_i}$ where \begin{itemize} \item $\delta_0 \in (0, \Delta(f, \crscode[\field, \evaldomain_0, m_0, \widehat{w}_0, \sigma_0]))$; \item the function $\gen(\parl; \alpha) = (1, \alpha, \dots, \alpha^{\parl-1})$ is a proximity generator with mutual correlated agreement for the codes $(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(i,s)})_{0 \leq i \leq M}^{0 \leq s \leq k_i}$ where $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(i,s)} := \rscode[\field, \evaldomain_i^{(2^s)}, m_i - s]$ with bound ${\bound}^\star$ and error $\err^\star$; \item for every $0 \leq i \le M$, $\delta_i \in (0, 1 - {\bound}^\star(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(i,s)}, 2))$; \item for every $0 \leq i \le M$, $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(i,s)}$ is $(\ell_{i,s}, \delta_i)$-list decodable. \end{itemize} Then there exists an IOPP for $\crscode[\field, \evaldomain_0, m_0, \widehat{w}_0, \sigma_0]$ with above parameters, with round-by-round soundness error \[ ((\varepsilon_{0,s}^{\mathrm{fold}})_{s \leq k_0},\ (\varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{out}},\ \varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{shift}})_{i \leq M},\ (\varepsilon_{i,s}^{\mathrm{fold}})_{i \in [M], s \leq k_i},\ \varepsilon^{\mathrm{fin}}), \] {where:} \begin{itemize} \item $\varepsilon_{0,s}^{\mathrm{fold}} \leq \dfrac{d^* \cdot \ell_{0,s-1}}{|\mathbb{F}|} + \mathrm{err}^*(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(0,s)}, 2, \delta_0)$; \item $\varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{out}} \leq \dfrac{2^{m_i} \cdot \ell_{i,0}^2}{2 \cdot |\mathbb{F}|}$; \item $\varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{shift}} \leq (1 - \delta_{i-1})^{t_i - 1} + \dfrac{\ell_{i,0} \cdot (t_i - 1 + 1)}{|\mathbb{F}|}$; \item $\varepsilon_{i,s}^{\mathrm{fold}} \leq \dfrac{d \cdot \ell_{i,s-1}}{|\mathbb{F}|} + \mathrm{err}^*(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(i,s)}, 2, \delta_i)$; \item $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{fin}} \leq (1 - \delta_{M-1})^{t_M - 1}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: WHIR is an IOPP for constrained RS codes with explicit round-by-round soundness errors per fold, out-of-domain, shift and final round.
nodes.label: thm: whir_rbr_soundness

nodes.name: Specification of Oracles
nodes.statement: An oracle specification describes a collection of available oracles, each with its own input and output types. Formally, it's given by an indexed family where each oracle is specified by: \begin{itemize} \item A domain type (what inputs it accepts) \item A range type (what outputs it can produce) \end{itemize} The indexing allows for potentially infinite collections of oracles, and the specification itself is agnostic to how the oracles actually behave - it just describes their interfaces.
nodes.label: def:oracle_spec

nodes.name: Examples of oracle specifications
nodes.statement: Some examples of oracle specifications (and their intended behavior) are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item \verb|emptySpec|: Represents an empty set of oracles \item \verb|singletonSpec|: Represents a single oracle available on a singleton index \item \verb|coinSpec|: A coin flipping oracle that produces a random Boolean value \item \verb|unifSpec|: A family of oracles that for every natural number $n \in \mathbb{N}$ chooses uniformly from the set $\{0, \ldots, n\}$.

nodes.name: Oracle Computation
nodes.statement: An oracle computation represents a program that can make oracle queries. It can: \begin{itemize} \item Return a pure value without making any queries (via \texttt{pure}) \item Make an oracle query and continue with the response (via \texttt{queryBind}) \item Signal failure (via \texttt{failure}) \end{itemize} The formal implementation uses a free monad on the inductive type of oracle queries wrapped in an option monad transformer (i.e. \verb|OptionT(FreeMonad(OracleQuery spec))|).
nodes.label: def:oracle_computation

nodes.name: Handling Oracle Queries
nodes.statement: To actually run oracle computations, we need a way to handle (or implement) the oracle queries. An oracle implementation consists a mapping from oracle queries to values in another monad. Depending on the monad, this may allow for various interpretations of the oracle queries.
nodes.label: def:handling_oracle_queries

nodes.name: Probabilistic Semantics of Oracle Computations
nodes.statement: We can view oracle computations as probabilistic programs by considering what happens when oracles respond uniformly at random. This gives rise to a probability distribution over possible outputs (including the possibility of failure). The semantics maps each oracle query to a uniform distribution over its possible responses.
nodes.label: def:probabilistic_semantics_of_oracle_computations

nodes.name: Simulating Oracle Queries with Other Oracles
nodes.statement: We can simulate complex oracles using simpler ones by providing a translation mechanism. A simulation oracle specifies how to implement queries in one specification using computations in another specification, possibly maintaining additional state information during the simulation.
nodes.label: def:sim_oracle

nodes.name: Logging \& Caching Oracle Queries
nodes.statement: Using the simulation framework, we can add logging and caching behaviors to oracle queries: \begin{itemize} \item Logging records all queries made during a computation \item Caching remembers query responses and reuses them for repeated queries \end{itemize} These are implemented as special cases of simulation oracles.
nodes.label: def:logging_caching_oracle_queries

nodes.name: Random Oracle
nodes.statement: A random oracle is implemented as a caching oracle that uses lazy sampling: \begin{itemize} \item On first query: generates a uniform random response and caches it \item On repeated queries: returns the cached response \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:random_oracle

nodes.name: Hachi setting
nodes.statement: Throughout, $d = 2^\alpha$, $R_q = \Z_q[X]/(X^{d}+1)$ with $q$ an odd prime, $k = 2^\kappa$ a divisor of $d/2$ (i.e.\ $2k \mid d$), and $H = \langle \sigma_{-1}, \sigma_{4k+1}\rangle$.

nodes.name: q congruent to 5 mod 8
nodes.statement: For the field statement we additionally assume $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$.

nodes.name: Fixed subring
nodes.statement: $R_q^H := \{x \in R_q : \sigma_{-1}(x) = x \wedge \sigma_{4k+1}(x) = x\}$, defined as the meet of two \texttt{eqLocus}'s, hence a \texttt{Subring}.
nodes.label: def:fixedSubring

nodes.name: Cardinality, Eq.~7
nodes.statement: Over $R = \Z_q$ with $q$ prime and $2k \mid d$, $\;|R_q^H| = q^{k}$.
assumptions: Over $R = \Z_q$ with $q$ prime and $2k \mid d$
nodes.label: thm:card_fixedSubring

nodes.name: Packing bijection, Theorem~2
nodes.statement: The map $\psi : (R_q^H)^{d/k} \to R_q$ is a bijection.
conclusions: The map $\psi : (R_q^H)^{d/k} \to R_q$ is a bijection.
nodes.label: thm:psi_bijective

nodes.name: Lemma 5: field isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be prime with $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $2 \cdot 2^\kappa \mid 2^\alpha$. Then there is a ring isomorphism \[ R_q^{H} \;\cong\; \F_{q^{2^\kappa}} \quad\bigl(\texttt{GaloisField } q\ (2^\kappa)\bigr). \]
assumptions: $q$ be prime with $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $2 \cdot 2^\kappa \mid 2^\alpha$
conclusions: there is a ring isomorphism
nodes.label: thm:fixedSubring_equiv_galoisField

nodes.name: Proof of the field isomorphism R_q^H = F_{q^{2^kappa}}
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:fixedSubring_isField} $R_q^H$ is a finite field, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:card_fixedSubring} it has cardinality $q^{2^\kappa}$. Any finite field of cardinality $q^{2^\kappa}$ is isomorphic to $\texttt{GaloisField } q\ (2^\kappa)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:finiteField_ringEquiv_of_card}).
nodes.statement_short: R_q^H is a finite field of cardinality q^(2^kappa), hence isomorphic to GaloisField q (2^kappa).

nodes.name: Finite field by cardinality
nodes.statement: Two finite fields of equal cardinality are isomorphic; in particular a finite field of cardinality $q^{n}$ is isomorphic to $\texttt{GaloisField } q\ n$. \emph{(Mathlib;} \texttt{GaloisField}/\texttt{FiniteField} \emph{API.)}
conclusions: Two finite fields of equal cardinality are isomorphic
a finite field of cardinality $q^{n}$ is isomorphic to $\texttt{GaloisField } q\ n$
nodes.label: lem:finiteField_ringEquiv_of_card

nodes.name: Subring of a domain is a domain
nodes.statement: If $S \le T$ is a subring of an integral domain $T$, then $S$ is an integral domain (it inherits \texttt{NoZeroDivisors}; \texttt{Mathlib}).
assumptions: $S \le T$ is a subring of an integral domain $T$
conclusions: $S$ is an integral domain
nodes.label: lem:subring_isDomain

nodes.name: Finite domain is a field
nodes.statement: A finite nontrivial commutative integral domain is a field. \emph{(Mathlib;} \texttt{Finite.isField\_of\_domain} \emph{/} \texttt{Fintype.fieldOfDomain}.\emph{)}
conclusions: A finite nontrivial commutative integral domain is a field.
nodes.label: lem:finite_domain_field

nodes.name: $R_q^H$ is a field
nodes.statement: For $q$ prime, $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, $2k \mid d$, the ring $R_q^H$ is a field.
assumptions: For $q$ prime, $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, $2k \mid d$
conclusions: the ring $R_q^H$ is a field
nodes.label: thm:fixedSubring_isField

nodes.name: Proof that R_q^H is a field
nodes.statement: $R_q^H \subseteq R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:fixedSubring_le_conjFixedSubring}), and $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$ is a field (Theorem~\ref{thm:conjFixedSubring_isField}). A subring of a field is an integral domain (Lemma~\ref{lem:subring_isDomain}); $R_q^H$ is finite (\texttt{fixedSubring.fintype}) and nontrivial, hence a field (Lemma~\ref{lem:finite_domain_field}).
nodes.statement_short: R_q^H sits in the field R_q^{sigma_-1}, so it is a finite domain, hence a field.

nodes.name: Conjugation-fixed subring $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$
nodes.statement: $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}} := \{x \in R_q : \sigma_{-1}(x) = x\} = \texttt{eqLocus}\ \sigma_{-1}\ \mathrm{id}$.
nodes.label: def:conjFixedSubring

nodes.name: $R_q^H \le R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$
nodes.statement: $R_q^H \subseteq R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$, immediate from the definition of $R_q^H$ as a meet whose first factor is $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$.
conclusions: $R_q^H \subseteq R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$
nodes.label: lem:fixedSubring_le_conjFixedSubring

nodes.name: Order of $q$ modulo the conductor
nodes.statement: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $\alpha \ge 1$, the multiplicative order of $q$ in $(\Z/2^{\alpha+1})^\times$ is $2^{\alpha-1}$.
assumptions: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $\alpha \ge 1$
conclusions: the multiplicative order of $q$ in $(\Z/2^{\alpha+1})^\times$ is $2^{\alpha-1}$
nodes.label: lem:order_q

nodes.name: Proof of the order of q
nodes.statement: $(\Z/2^{\alpha+1})^\times \cong \langle -1\rangle \times \langle 5\rangle$ with $|\langle 5\rangle| = 2^{\alpha-1}$. Writing $q \equiv (-1)^a 5^b$, the congruence $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ forces $a = 0$ and $b$ odd; since $b$ is odd it is a unit mod $2^{\alpha-1}$, so $q$ generates $\langle 5\rangle$ and $\operatorname{ord}(q) = 2^{\alpha-1}$. The $2$-adic computation is the same lifting-the-exponent toolkit already used in \texttt{Galois/Order.lean} (\texttt{two\_pow\_dvd\_four\_pow\_sub\_one\_iff}).
nodes.statement_short: Use (Z/2^(a+1))^x = <-1> x <5>; q = 5 mod 8 forces q to generate <5>, of order 2^(a-1).

nodes.name: Two irreducible factors
nodes.statement: Over $\F_q$ with $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, the polynomial $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = \Phi_{2^{\alpha+1}}(X)$ factors as a product of exactly two distinct monic irreducible polynomials, each of degree $2^{\alpha-1} = d/2$.
assumptions: Over $\F_q$ with $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$
conclusions: the polynomial $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = \Phi_{2^{\alpha+1}}(X)$ factors as a product of exactly two distinct monic irreducible polynomials, each of degree $2^{\alpha-1} = d/2$
nodes.label: lem:two_factors

nodes.name: Proof of the two-factor decomposition
nodes.statement: $X^{2^\alpha}+1$ is the $2^{\alpha+1}$-th cyclotomic polynomial. Since $q \nmid 2^{\alpha+1}$ it is separable over $\F_q$, and over a finite field every irreducible factor of $\Phi_n$ has degree $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)$; the number of factors is $\varphi(n)/\operatorname{ord}_n(q)$. With $n = 2^{\alpha+1}$, $\varphi(n) = 2^\alpha$ and $\operatorname{ord}_n(q) = 2^{\alpha-1}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:order_q}), giving exactly $2$ factors of degree $2^{\alpha-1}$. Formalized directly from Mathlib's \texttt{Polynomial.normalizedFactors\_cyclotomic\_card} (factor count $= \varphi(n)/\operatorname{ord}$) together with \texttt{Nat.totient\_prime\_pow\_succ}.
nodes.statement_short: Cyclotomic factorization over F_q: phi(n)/ord_n(q) = 2 factors of degree ord_n(q) = 2^(a-1).

nodes.name: Factor existence
nodes.statement: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = p_1 \cdot p_2$ over $\F_q$ with $p_1, p_2$ coprime and irreducible. (Extracted from the two normalized factors; coprimality of the distinct monic irreducibles via \texttt{Irreducible.coprime\_iff\_not\_dvd}.)
assumptions: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$
conclusions: $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = p_1 \cdot p_2$ over $\F_q$ with $p_1, p_2$ coprime and irreducible
nodes.label: lem:factorization

nodes.name: Quotient ring S
nodes.statement: Rather than build the explicit CRT product $K \times K$, we work directly in $S := \F_q[X]/(X^{2^\alpha}+1)$ via a \emph{reverse identity} and a divisibility argument.

nodes.name: The reverse identity
nodes.statement: In $S$, with $\mathrm{mk}$ the quotient map and $\sigma_{-1} = \texttt{galoisAutₛ}$ of exponent $2^{\alpha+1}-1$, \[ \mathrm{mk}(p^{\mathrm{rev}}) \;=\; \sigma_{-1}(\mathrm{mk}\,p)\cdot(\mathrm{mk}\,X)^{\deg p}. \] Since $\mathrm{mk}\,X$ is a unit, $\sigma_{-1}$ carries the ideal $(\mathrm{mk}\,p)$ onto $(\mathrm{mk}\,p^{\mathrm{rev}})$. Proved from Mathlib's \texttt{Polynomial.eval₂\_reverse\_mul\_pow} at the point $(\mathrm{mk}\,X)^{-1} = (\mathrm{mk}\,X)^{c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial reversal in S equals sigma_{-1} applied, times a power of the unit X.
nodes.label: lem:conj_reverse

nodes.name: No self-reciprocal factor
nodes.statement: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, reversal swaps the two factors: if $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = p_1 p_2$ with $p_1, p_2$ irreducible, then $p_1^{\mathrm{rev}}$ is associated to $p_2$. This is the step carrying the $-1 \notin \langle q\rangle$ root-orbit content. The root set of $p_1$ is a single Frobenius orbit $=$ a coset of $\langle q\rangle$; were $p_1^{\mathrm{rev}} \sim p_1$ it would be closed under $\zeta \mapsto \zeta^{-1}$, i.e.\ $-1 \in \langle q\rangle$, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:neg_one_notMem}; as reversal permutes the two factors of the self-reciprocal $X^{2^\alpha}+1$, it sends $p_1$ to $p_2$.
assumptions: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$
if $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = p_1 p_2$ with $p_1, p_2$ irreducible
conclusions: $p_1^{\mathrm{rev}}$ is associated to $p_2$
nodes.label: lem:no_selfReciprocal

nodes.name: $-1 \notin \langle q\rangle$
nodes.statement: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $\alpha \ge 1$, no power of $q$ equals $-1$ in $\Z/2^{\alpha+1}$ (every power is $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, while $-1 \equiv 3$).
assumptions: For $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $\alpha \ge 1$
conclusions: no power of $q$ equals $-1$ in $\Z/2^{\alpha+1}$
nodes.label: lem:neg_one_notMem

nodes.name: Core unit lemma
nodes.statement: In $S = \F_q[X]/(X^{2^\alpha}+1)$ every nonzero $\sigma_{-1}$-fixed element is a unit.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
conclusions: every nonzero $\sigma_{-1}$-fixed element is a unit
nodes.label: thm:core_unit

nodes.name: Proof of the core unit lemma
nodes.statement: Write the element as $\mathrm{mk}\,g$. If it is not a unit then $g$ is not coprime to $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = p_1 p_2$, so (WLOG) $p_1 \mid g$. The reverse identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:conj_reverse}) together with $p_1^{\mathrm{rev}} \sim p_2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:no_selfReciprocal}) gives $\mathrm{mk}\,p_2 \mid \sigma_{-1}(\mathrm{mk}\,p_1) \mid \sigma_{-1}(\mathrm{mk}\,g) = \mathrm{mk}\,g$, hence $p_2 \mid g$. With $p_1 \mid g$ and $p_1, p_2$ coprime, $X^{2^\alpha}+1 \mid g$, so $\mathrm{mk}\,g = 0$ --- contradiction.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: A non-unit fixed element is divisible by p1, hence via reversal by p2, hence by X^(2^a)+1, so it is 0.

nodes.name: $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$ is a field
nodes.statement: For $q$ prime with $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $\alpha \ge 1$, $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$ is a field.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
assumptions: For $q$ prime with $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ and $\alpha \ge 1$
conclusions: $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$ is a field
nodes.label: thm:conjFixedSubring_isField

nodes.name: Proof that R_q^{sigma_-1} is a field
nodes.statement: Transport along $R_q \cong S$ (\texttt{Rq.equivQuotient}), under which $\sigma_{-1}$ becomes $\texttt{galoisAutₛ}$ (\texttt{galoisAut\_toQuotient}). A nonzero $\sigma_{-1}$-fixed element of $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$ maps to a nonzero fixed element of $S$, a unit by Theorem~\ref{thm:core_unit}; its inverse is again $\sigma_{-1}$-fixed (apply $\sigma_{-1}$ to $a a^{-1} = 1$ and cancel the unit), so it lies in $R_q^{\sigma_{-1}}$.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Transport to S, where nonzero fixed elements are units; inverses stay fixed.

nodes.name: Prover sends round polynomial
nodes.statement: the prover sends a univariate polynomial of bounded degree
nodes.statement_short: Prover sends a bounded-degree univariate polynomial.

nodes.name: Verifier sends challenge
nodes.statement: the verifier responds with a random challenge
nodes.statement_short: Verifier replies with a random challenge.

nodes.name: Consistency checks
nodes.statement: The verifier performs consistency checks by querying the polynomial oracle at specific evaluation points.
nodes.statement_short: Verifier checks consistency via evaluation queries.

nodes.name: Output evaluation claim
nodes.statement: After $n$ rounds, the protocol terminates with an output statement asserting that $P(r_0, r_1, \ldots, r_{n-1}) = e$, where the challenges $(r_0, r_1, \ldots, r_{n-1})$ are the random values chosen by the verifier during the protocol execution.
nodes.statement_short: Output the claim P(r) = e.

nodes.name: Prover sends s_i
nodes.statement: in each round $i$ the prover sends a univariate polynomial $s_i$ of bounded degree
nodes.statement_short: Prover sends the round polynomial s_i.

nodes.name: Verifier sends r_i
nodes.statement: the verifier sends a challenge $r_i \gets \mathbb{F}$
nodes.statement_short: Verifier samples and sends r_i.

nodes.name: Honest prover computation
nodes.statement: The honest prover would compute \[ s_i(X) = \sum_{x \in \{0, 1\}^{n - i - 1}} P(r_1, \ldots, r_{i - 1}, X, x), \]
nodes.statement_short: Honest s_i sums P over the remaining Boolean variables.

nodes.name: Verifier check
nodes.statement: the honest verifier would check that $s_i(0) + s_i(1) = s_{i - 1}(r_{i - 1})$, with the convention that $s_0(r_0) = c$

nodes.name: Step 1: Prover's message
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Step 1: Prover's Message.} The prover sends a univariate polynomial $p_i \in R[X]_{\leq d}$ of degree at most $d$. If the prover is honest, then: \[ p_i(X) = \sum_{x \in (\text{Image}(\mathcal{D}))^{n-i}} P(\text{challenges}_0, \ldots, \text{challenges}_{i-1}, X, x) \] Here, $P(\text{challenges}_0, \ldots, \text{challenges}_{i-1}, X, x)$ is the polynomial $P$ evaluated at the concatenation of: \begin{itemize} \item the prior challenges $\text{challenges}_0, \ldots, \text{challenges}_{i-1}$ \item the $i$-th variable as the new indeterminate $X$ \item the remaining values $x \in (\text{Image}(\mathcal{D}))^{n-i}$ \end{itemize} In the oracle protocol, this polynomial $p_i$ is turned into an oracle for which the verifier can query evaluations at arbitrary points.
nodes.statement_short: Prover sends the partial-sum univariate p_i as an oracle.

nodes.name: Step 2: Verifier's challenge
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Step 2: Verifier's Challenge.} The verifier sends the $i$-th challenge $r_i$ sampled uniformly at random from $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Verifier samples r_i uniformly.

nodes.name: Step 3: Verifier's check
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Step 3: Verifier's Check.} The (oracle) verifier performs queries for the evaluations of $p_i$ at all points in $\text{Image}(\mathcal{D})$, and checks that: \[ \sum_{x \in \text{Image}(\mathcal{D})} p_i(x) = \text{target} \] If the check fails, the verifier outputs $\texttt{failure}$. Otherwise, it outputs a statement for the next round as follows: \begin{itemize} \item $\text{target}$ is updated to $p_i(r_i)$ \item $\text{challenges}$ is updated to the concatenation of the previous challenges and $r_i$
nodes.statement_short: Check the domain sum of p_i equals target; output updated target and challenges.

nodes.name: Prover's message
nodes.statement: \textbf{Prover's message:} A univariate polynomial $p_i \in R[X]_{\leq d}$
nodes.statement_short: Prover sends p_i.

nodes.name: Verifier's challenge
nodes.statement: \textbf{Verifier's challenge:} A random element $r_i \gets R$
nodes.statement_short: Verifier samples r_i.

nodes.name: Output
nodes.statement: \textbf{Output:} An updated statement with new target $p_i(r_i)$ and extended challenges
nodes.statement_short: Output the updated statement.

nodes.name: Context and relation
nodes.statement: In this protocol, the context is a pair $(p, d)$, where $p$ is now a \emph{univariate} polynomial of bounded degree. The predicate / relation is that $p(0) + p(1) = d$.
nodes.statement_short: Context (p, d) with relation p(0)+p(1)=d.

nodes.name: Prover sends s
nodes.statement: The prover first sends a univariate polynomial $s$ of the same bounded degree as $p$. In the honest case, it would just send $p$ itself.
nodes.statement_short: Prover sends s (honestly p).

nodes.name: Verifier sends r
nodes.statement: The verifier samples and sends a random challenge $r \gets R$.
nodes.statement_short: Verifier samples r.

nodes.name: Verifier check
nodes.statement: The verifier checks that $s(0) + s(1) = d$. The predicate on the resulting output context is that $p(r) = s(r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Check s(0)+s(1)=d; output predicate p(r)=s(r).

nodes.name: Batching
nodes.statement: \textbf{Batching} (). The prover sends the folded element $\hat s \in A$. The verifier checks the original claim against its column-decomposition, $s = \sum_v \tilde{\mathrm{eq}}(v, r_{0..\kappa-1})\cdot \mathrm{decomposeColumns}(\hat s)_v$, then sends a batching challenge $r'' \in L^\kappa$, collapsing the $\kappa$ packed coordinates into a single sum-check target $s_0 = \sum_u \tilde{\mathrm{eq}}(u, r'')\cdot \mathrm{decomposeRows}(\hat s)_u$. (Soundness loss $\kappa/\lvert L\rvert$.)
nodes.statement_short: Send folded element, check column decomposition, batch rows with r''.

nodes.name: Sum-check
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sum-check} (). A degree-$2$ multilinear sum-check over $L$ on $H = A_{\mathrm{MLE}} \cdot t'$, over $\ell'$ rounds plus a final round, reducing the sum claim to a single evaluation of $t'$ at a random point. (Loss $2/\lvert L\rvert$ per round, $1/\lvert L\rvert$ final.)
nodes.statement_short: Degree-2 multilinear sum-check over L on A_MLE * t'.

nodes.name: Opening
nodes.statement: \textbf{Opening}. The residual evaluation claim about $t'$ over $L$ is discharged by the underlying large-field multilinear IOPCS.
nodes.statement_short: Discharge the residual evaluation claim with the large-field IOPCS.

nodes.name: Send witness oracle
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{P}$: Sends oracle access to the multilinear extension of the witness, $\tilde{w}$, to $\mathcal{V}$. In the original paper, this is a commitment $(C,S) \leftarrow \text{PC.Commit}(\text{pp}, \tilde{w})$.

nodes.name: Sample tau
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Samples a random challenge $\tau \in \mathbb{F}^{\log m}$ and sends it to $\mathcal{P}$.

nodes.name: Sum-check #1 parameters
nodes.statement: Let $T_1 = 0$, $\mu_1 = \log m$, $\ell_1 = 3$. These are parameters for the first sum-check protocol.

nodes.name: Sample r_x
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Samples a random challenge $r_x \in \mathbb{F}^{\mu_1}$.

nodes.name: Sum-check #1
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sum-check\#1.} A sum-check protocol is executed. The verifier receives the claimed evaluation $e_x$. The prover of the sum-check has oracle access to a polynomial $G_{io, \tau}$, and the verifier has oracle access to $r_x$. The parameters for this sub-protocol are $(\mu_1, \ell_1, T_1)$.

nodes.name: Send v_A, v_B, v_C
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{P}$: Computes evaluations $v_A = \tilde{A}(r_x)$, $v_B = \tilde{B}(r_x)$, $v_C = \tilde{C}(r_x)$ and sends them to $\mathcal{V}$. $\tilde{A}, \tilde{B}, \tilde{C}$ are multilinear extensions of the matrices $A, B, C$.

nodes.name: Check e_x
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Aborts if $e_x \neq (v_A \cdot v_B - v_C) \cdot \tilde{\text{eq}}(r_x, \tau)$. This is the verifier's check for the first sum-check.

nodes.name: Sample r_A, r_B, r_C
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Samples random challenges $r_A, r_B, r_C \in \mathbb{F}$ and sends them to $\mathcal{P}$.

nodes.name: Sum-check #2 parameters
nodes.statement: Let $T_2 = r_A \cdot v_A + r_B \cdot v_B + r_C \cdot v_C$, $\mu_2 = \log n$, $\ell_2 = 2$. These are parameters for the second sum-check protocol. Note: The image states $\mu_2 = \log m$, which is likely a typo and should be $\log n$.

nodes.name: Sample r_y
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Samples a random challenge $r_y \in \mathbb{F}^{\mu_2}$.

nodes.name: Sum-check #2
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sum-check\#2.} Another sum-check protocol is executed. The verifier receives the claimed evaluation $e_y$.

nodes.name: Send v
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{P}$: Computes $v \leftarrow \tilde{w}(r_y[1..])$ and sends $v$ to $\mathcal{V}$.

nodes.name: PCS evaluation proof (omitted)
nodes.statement: This step involves a polynomial commitment evaluation proof. In our PIOP formalization, this check is not needed as the verifier has direct oracle access to $\tilde{w}$.

nodes.name: Evaluation proof check (omitted)
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: This step is part of the evaluation proof check, so it is omitted.

nodes.name: Compute v_Z
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Computes $v_Z \leftarrow (1 - r_y[0]) \cdot \tilde{w}(r_y[1..]) + r_y[0] \cdot \widetilde{(\text{io}, 1)}(r_y[1..])$. This reconstructs the evaluation of the combined input-witness vector polynomial $\tilde{z}$.

nodes.name: Query matrix oracles
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Queries oracles for $\tilde{A}, \tilde{B}, \tilde{C}$ at $(r_x, r_y)$ to get $v_1, v_2, v_3$.

nodes.name: Final check
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Aborts if $e_y \neq (r_A \cdot v_1 + r_B \cdot v_2 + r_C \cdot v_3) \cdot v_Z$. This is the final check.

nodes.name: Accept
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{V}$: Outputs 1.

nodes.name: Structure of the unit group
nodes.statement: $(\Z/2^{\alpha+1})^\times \cong \langle -1\rangle \times \langle 5\rangle$ with $|\langle 5\rangle| = 2^{\alpha-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the unit group decomposition.

nodes.name: Order of q
nodes.statement: Writing $q \equiv (-1)^a 5^b$, the congruence $q \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ forces $a = 0$ and $b$ odd; since $b$ is odd it is a unit mod $2^{\alpha-1}$, so $q$ generates $\langle 5\rangle$ and $\operatorname{ord}(q) = 2^{\alpha-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: q = 5 mod 8 forces a=0, b odd, so ord(q)=2^(a-1).

nodes.name: Formalization note
nodes.statement: The $2$-adic computation is the same lifting-the-exponent toolkit already used in \texttt{Galois/Order.lean} (\texttt{two\_pow\_dvd\_four\_pow\_sub\_one\_iff}).
nodes.statement_short: Same LTE toolkit as Galois/Order.lean.

nodes.name: Cyclotomic identification
nodes.statement: $X^{2^\alpha}+1$ is the $2^{\alpha+1}$-th cyclotomic polynomial.
nodes.statement_short: Identify X^(2^a)+1 as a cyclotomic polynomial.

nodes.name: Factor degrees over finite fields
nodes.statement: Since $q \nmid 2^{\alpha+1}$ it is separable over $\F_q$, and over a finite field every irreducible factor of $\Phi_n$ has degree $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)$; the number of factors is $\varphi(n)/\operatorname{ord}_n(q)$.
nodes.statement_short: Irreducible factors of Phi_n have degree ord_n(q).

nodes.name: Count factors
nodes.statement: With $n = 2^{\alpha+1}$, $\varphi(n) = 2^\alpha$ and $\operatorname{ord}_n(q) = 2^{\alpha-1}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:order_q}), giving exactly $2$ factors of degree $2^{\alpha-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Plug in phi(n) and ord_n(q) to get two factors.

nodes.name: Formalization note
nodes.statement: Formalized directly from Mathlib's \texttt{Polynomial.normalizedFactors\_cyclotomic\_card} (factor count $= \varphi(n)/\operatorname{ord}$) together with \texttt{Nat.totient\_prime\_pow\_succ}.
nodes.statement_short: Mathlib lemmas used.

nodes.name: Assume non-unit
nodes.statement: Write the element as $\mathrm{mk}\,g$. If it is not a unit then $g$ is not coprime to $X^{2^\alpha}+1 = p_1 p_2$, so (WLOG) $p_1 \mid g$.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Suppose mk g is not a unit; then WLOG p1 divides g.

nodes.name: Apply the swap
nodes.statement: The reverse identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:conj_reverse}) together with $p_1^{\mathrm{rev}} \sim p_2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:no_selfReciprocal}) gives $\mathrm{mk}\,p_2 \mid \sigma_{-1}(\mathrm{mk}\,p_1) \mid \sigma_{-1}(\mathrm{mk}\,g) = \mathrm{mk}\,g$, hence $p_2 \mid g$.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Reverse identity and the factor swap give p2 | g.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: With $p_1 \mid g$ and $p_1, p_2$ coprime, $X^{2^\alpha}+1 \mid g$, so $\mathrm{mk}\,g = 0$ --- contradiction.
nodes.section: 5.4.6 Phase 5: assembling the field and the isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Both factors divide g, so mk g = 0.
